<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, this project is a cross-platform screen sharing tool built using Electron with a Svelte-based renderer. The application leverages a peer-to-peer connection (WebRTC) for screen sharing while relying on external STUN, TURN, and signaling servers to bootstrap the connection. Below are the guidelines for constructing an accurate and detailed system design diagram tailored to this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Electron Main Process: This is found under src/main (files like index.ts, ipcMainHandlers.ts, stateKeeper.ts, and utils.ts). It orchestrates the application’s lifecycle, manages native integrations (e.g., screen capture), and handles IPC communication.
   • Preload Process: Under src/preload, the preload scripts expose controlled, secure APIs to the renderer process. This acts as the bridge between the main process and the renderer.
   • Renderer Process: The UI is built with Svelte and lives inside src/renderer (including HTML, Svelte components, and accompanying assets and style files). This component displays the application interface and interacts with the main process via the preload scripts.
   • Internationalization (i18n): The src/i18n directory contains modules for multiple languages (de, en, fr, zh) along with utilities and configuration to provide localized UI support.
   • Build & Packaging Infrastructure: Tools and configuration files like electron-builder.yml, electron.vite.config.ts, package.json, and several scripts in the scripts/ directory indicate build, versioning, and release automation processes.
   • External Communication: Though not in the file tree explicitly as a module, the README references the use of STUN/TURN and signaling servers to set up the peer-to-peer connection. Represent these as external components that the application communicates with.

2. Diagram Components and Relationships:
   • Draw a container or module labeled “Electron App” to encapsulate the internal components.
   • Inside the container, separate the application into:
     - Main Process (src/main): Label important functions, including IPC handling.
     - Preload Scripts (src/preload): Indicate their role as a secure bridge.
     - Renderer Process (src/renderer): Show that this is where the Svelte-based UI logic resides.
     - Internationalization Layer (src/i18n): Connect it to the renderer and possibly the main process if localization is applied during startup.
   • Illustrate arrows from the Renderer to the Preload and then to the Main Process to depict the data flow and secure communication channel provided by Electron’s isolation model.
   • From the Main Process, draw arrows toward “External Services,” which represent the STUN, TURN, and signaling servers used during the peer-to-peer connection handshake.
   • Additionally, include a “Build & Deployment Pipeline” component to represent the scripts and configurations that bundle, release, and notarize the application (using tools such as electron-builder).

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Technologies:
   • Separation of Concerns: Distinct boundaries exist between the main process, preload scripts, and the renderer (Svelte UI). This follows Electron’s recommended architecture for security and maintainability.
   • IPC (Inter-Process Communication): Emphasize the role of IPC channels (as seen in src/main/ipcMainHandlers.ts) which are critical in the interaction between frontend and backend layers within the Electron app.
   • TypeScript and Svelte: Mention that the use of TypeScript (as indicated by tsconfig files) provides type safety across the project, and Svelte ensures a streamlined UI layer.
   • Internationalization: The i18n directory shows the commitment to multi-language support, with modules handling different languages and formats.

4. Tailoring the Diagram:
   • Use clear labels and group related files into components, so it is immediately obvious which files back a particular layer (e.g., grouping the content under src/main, src/preload, and src/renderer).
   • Incorporate directional arrows to represent the flow of data and control signals— for example, arrows from renderer → preload → main, and from main → external services.
   • Use colors or different shapes (e.g., rectangles for processes, cylinders for external servers, rounded boxes for UI components) to visually distinguish between types of elements.
   • Clearly label all components (like “Main Process”, “Renderer (Svelte UI)”, “Preload Scripts”, “i18n Modules”, “External Signaling Servers”, and “Build & Deployment Pipeline”).

5. Additional Guidelines:
   • Be detailed: Don’t hesitate to break down components further if necessary. For example, within the renderer, you might isolate key UI components such as “About.svelte”, “Settings.svelte”, “WebRTC.svelte”, etc., to emphasize the distinct roles they play.
   • Capture essential build and deployment processes: Show how scripts (e.g., build.sh, release.sh, and set-version.sh) integrate with the overall lifecycle of the application.
   • Ensure consistency in visual language: Use consistent arrow styles and color codes so the relationship between the UI, backend, and external services is easily comprehensible.

By following this structured approach, you will produce a detailed system design diagram that accurately represents the architecture of Bananas Screen Sharing, offering a clear view of its main components, their interactions, and the underlying technologies. This diagram will help stakeholders (and future developers) understand how the system is structured and how its different parts work together to enable simple, peer-to-peer screen sharing across platforms.
</explanation>
